meta.titre: World Wide Web: telling the Web from the Internet, intranets and extranets
meta.sous_theme: Internet versus WWW, web and email addresses, intranet and extranet, browser and search engine

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Computer Science past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A printer owner in Bamenda sends an invoice to a client by email and then checks the price of paper on a supplier's web page. Both jobs use the Internet, but they use two different services running on it. Many candidates write that the Internet and the Web are the same thing, and the GCE keeps asking for the difference, together with questions on email addresses, intranets and browsers. A clear definition of each term, followed by one contrast, wins these marks.

items: A network is a group of computers and devices joined together so that they can share data.
A web browser such as Chrome or Firefox is a program used to display web pages.
Web pages are written in HTML, a language made of tags.

sections.titre: The Internet, the Web and private networks
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Internet and World Wide Web

The **Internet** is a worldwide network of networks. It is made of the computers, cables, routers and wireless links that connect millions of devices, and it carries many services such as email, file transfer, online calls and the Web.

The **World Wide Web (WWW)** is one of those services: a huge collection of web pages stored on web servers and joined together by hyperlinks. Pages are requested and displayed with a browser, using the rules (the protocol) called **HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol). **HTTPS** is the secure version, which encrypts the data sent between the browser and the server.

| | Internet | World Wide Web |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | The global network itself (hardware and connections) | A service made of linked pages and sites, carried by that network |
| Made of | Computers, cables, routers, links | Web pages, websites, hyperlinks, web servers |
| Used for | Email, file transfer, calls, the Web | Viewing pages and following links in a browser |

The Web needs the Internet to work, but the Internet can work without the Web: email alone is an example.

### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Web page | One document on the Web, written in HTML |
| Website | A group of related web pages under one domain name |
| Web server | A computer that stores web pages and sends them when asked |
| Hyperlink | Text or a picture that opens another page when clicked |
| ISP | Internet Service Provider: the company that connects you to the Internet |
| Domain name | The readable name of a site, such as `greenfield.example` |

### Parts of an address

A web address (URL) such as `https://www.greenfield.example/news/exams.html` has three parts: the protocol (`https`), the domain name (`www.greenfield.example`) and the path to the page (`/news/exams.html`). An email address such as `mary.ndi@greenfield.example` has two parts separated by the `@` sign: the **username** (`mary.ndi`) before it and the **domain name** (`greenfield.example`) after it.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question compares private networks with the Internet
variantes.contenu_markdown: An **intranet** is a private network that uses Internet technology (browsers and web pages) but can be used only by the members of one organisation, for example the staff of a school who read internal notices. An **extranet** extends an intranet to selected outsiders, such as suppliers or parents, who log in to reach a limited part of it. The **Internet** is public and open to everyone. Ordering by access: intranet (members only), extranet (members plus approved guests), Internet (everybody).

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks you to separate two tools used on the Web
variantes.contenu_markdown: A **browser** is the software on your device that requests web pages and displays them (Chrome, Firefox, Edge). A **search engine** is a website, such as Google or Bing, that keeps an index of pages and returns a list of links matching the words you type. You use a browser to reach a search engine, not the other way round.

Define the first term, define the second, then join them with a contrast word such as *whereas*. Give both sides: an answer that only explains one term earns half the marks. One example in brackets can support each definition.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A student of Greenfield College sends a report to a teacher at `mary.ndi@greenfield.example`, then opens `https://www.greenfield.example/library/books.html` in a browser. The college also has a private site that only its teachers and students can open.

(a) Name the username and the domain name in the email address.

(b) Name the protocol and the path in the web address.

(c) State one difference between the Internet and the WWW.

(d) What type of network is the college's private site?

etapes.action: Split the email address at the @ sign.
etapes.justification: The part before @ is the username and the part after is the domain name.

etapes.action: Split the web address into protocol, domain and path.
etapes.justification: The protocol comes before `://`, the domain name follows, and the path starts at the next slash.

etapes.action: Define each term, then contrast them.
etapes.justification: A difference question needs both sides.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The Internet is the worldwide network of connected computers, whereas the WWW is a service on it made of linked web pages.

etapes.action: Decide who may use the private site.
etapes.justification: A private network that uses Internet technology and is limited to members of one organisation is an intranet.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) Username `mary.ndi`; domain name `greenfield.example`. (b) Protocol `https`; path `/library/books.html`. (c) The Internet is the global network of cables, routers and computers, whereas the WWW is a collection of linked web pages carried over that network. (d) An intranet; it becomes an extranet only if approved outsiders, such as parents, are allowed in with a login.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that the Internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing.
items.pourquoi_faux: The Web is only one service on the Internet. Email and file transfer also use the Internet but are not web pages.
items.correction_markdown: The Internet is the network; the WWW is the linked pages carried on it.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving Google as an example of a browser, or Chrome as an example of a search engine.
items.pourquoi_faux: A browser displays pages, whereas a search engine finds pages. Google is a search engine and Chrome is a browser.
items.correction_markdown: Browser: Chrome, Firefox, Edge. Search engine: Google, Bing.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that the username in `kofi.t@school.example` is `school.example`.
items.pourquoi_faux: The username is the part before the @ sign. The part after it names the mail domain.

items.erreur_markdown: Describing an intranet as a smaller copy of the Internet that anyone can join.
items.pourquoi_faux: An intranet is private. Only the members of the organisation, or approved guests in an extranet, may use it.
items.correction_markdown: An intranet is a private network for one organisation, using Internet technology.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that the browser stores all the web pages of the world.
items.pourquoi_faux: Web pages are stored on web servers. The browser only requests them and displays them.
items.correction_markdown: Pages are kept on web servers; the browser fetches and shows them.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) For each item say whether it is part of the Internet itself or of the World Wide Web: a router joining two networks, a hyperlink that opens another page, a web server holding a school's home page.

(b) Name the username and the domain name in `paul.nkeng@mail-hub.example`.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) A router joining two networks is part of the **Internet** (hardware and connections). A hyperlink is part of the **WWW**. A web server holding a home page is part of the **WWW**, although it reaches users through the Internet.

(b) Username: **paul.nkeng**. Domain name: **mail-hub.example**.

items.enonce_markdown:
Esther wants a recipe for ndole. She opens Firefox, goes to the Bing website, types *ndole recipe* and clicks the second link in the list.

(a) Name the browser and the search engine.
(b) State what each of them did in this task.
(c) Where is the page she finally reads stored?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Browser: **Firefox**. Search engine: **Bing**.

(b) Firefox requested the pages from the web servers and displayed them on the screen. Bing searched its index for pages matching the words *ndole recipe* and returned a list of links.

(c) The page is stored on a **web server**, which sends it to the browser when requested.

items.enonce_markdown:
A company in Douala runs three online services: (i) pages about its products that anybody can read, (ii) an order-tracking page that its suppliers reach after entering a user name and password, (iii) a staff page with the salary policy that only employees may open.

For each service, state whether it is best described as part of the public Internet/Web, an extranet or an intranet, and give a reason. Then say why the login page of the supplier service should use HTTPS.
items.solution_markdown:
(i) **Public Web (Internet).** Anybody can open the pages, so no restriction is applied.

(ii) **Extranet.** Outside suppliers are allowed in, but only after logging in and only to a limited part of the company's system.

(iii) **Intranet.** Only employees may use it, so access is restricted to members of the organisation.

A supplier cannot open service (iii) because the extranet gives guests access to a limited part only. The login page should use **HTTPS** because it encrypts the user name and password, so that someone watching the connection cannot read them.

items_markdown: The Internet is the worldwide network of networks; the WWW is a service on it made of web pages joined by hyperlinks.
Web pages are stored on web servers, requested with HTTP or HTTPS, and shown by a browser.
A browser displays pages; a search engine finds pages by keywords.
In an email address the username is before the @ sign and the domain name is after it.
An intranet is private to one organisation, an extranet adds approved outsiders, and the Internet is open to all.
